newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan refugees short of food, drinking water.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan refugees short of food, drinking water.

text.p: Thousands of Tamil refugees displaced by fighting in northern Sri Lanka are still suffering from a lack of food and safe drinking water and from disease, aid officials say.

Food is not reaching some of an estimated 200,000 refugees because of problems in distribution in the Tamil rebel-held northern Wanni mainland despite the resumption of daily food convoys, the aid workers said over the weekend.

"Quite a lot of food is going across but some groups of refugees not registered with government authorities and not entitled to food rations are not getting enough food," said Frances Stevenson of Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF).

"We've seen signs of undernutrition, especially among children, because food distribution is patchy and some refugees not entitled to food rations go for days without proper food if they don't have money to buy it," she told Reuters.
Many of the refugees, displaced by fighting between the army and Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) in July, live in temporary shelters put up by aid agencies.
Others live under trees or in cramped conditions with friends and relations.
The refugees abandoned their homes when government forces launched an assault on LTTE positions in the town of Kilinochchi, 285 km (175 miles) north of Colombo.
The Tigers, fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east, set up base in Kilinochchi after the army captured their northern Jaffna peninsula stronghold in April.

Government forces are currently dug in north of Kilinochchi while the rebels have kept up sporadic hit-and-run attacks since they overran a northeastern army camp in July, killing or capturing almost its entire garrison of 1,400 men.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the ethnic war, now in its 14th year.

Arve Ofstad, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) representative, said there would not have been any food shortage for refugees after the army lifted a three-week blockade in mid-August, had it not been for the distribution problems.
"Since the resumption of food convoys our impression is that sufficient food is going into the area," he told Reuters. "But there may be gaps because of difficulties in distribution."
Ofstad said the U.N.'s main concern was adequate access to safe drinking water and a reported increase in cases of diarrhoea among refugees.
The MSF's Stevenson said malaria was on the increase because of a shortage of anti-malarial drugs in the region and the disruption of an anti-malaria campaign.
Aid officials said a truce between the Tigers and government forces on Friday and Saturday to help implement an island-wide polio immunisation programme appeared to have held.
Brita Ostberg, the United Nations Children's Emergency Fund representative in Sri Lanka, said she had appealed to the LTTE and the military to stop fighting on those days.
Last week, the UNDP said it would provide $267,000 to develop a programme to rehabilitate Jaffna after talks with the people and local authorities in the devastated peninsula.
The United States also announced last week that it had given $1.1 million for refugee rehabilitation work in Sri Lanka through the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees.
